title: 1. Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

q.t: What are the coordinates of the origin?
q.e: The origin is where the axes cross: zero distance from both axes, so both coordinates are 0.

q.t: What is the x-coordinate of the point (4, −7)?
q.e: The x-coordinate is always written first. It is the signed distance from the y-axis.

q.t: What is the y-coordinate of the point (4, −7)?
q.e: The y-coordinate is written second. −7 means 7 units below the x-axis.

q.t: In which quadrant does (−3, 5) lie?
q.e: x is negative (left of the y-axis) and y is positive (above the x-axis): left and up is Quadrant II.

q.t: In which quadrant does (6, −2) lie?
q.e: x positive (right), y negative (down): right and down is Quadrant IV.

q.t: The point (0, −3) lies:
q.e: Its x-coordinate is 0, so it is zero distance from the y-axis — it sits on the y-axis. Points on an axis are in no quadrant.

q.t: The point (5, 0) lies:
q.e: Its y-coordinate is 0, so it is zero distance from the x-axis — it sits on the x-axis.

q.t: How far is (3, −4) from the x-axis (in units)?
q.e: The distance from the x-axis is the size of the y-coordinate: |−4| = 4.

q.t: The horizontal axis of the Cartesian plane is called the:
q.e: By convention the horizontal number line is the x-axis and the vertical one is the y-axis.

q.t: Into how many quadrants do the axes divide the plane?
q.e: Left/right of the y-axis (2 choices) × above/below the x-axis (2 choices) = 4 regions.

q.t: How far is (−6, 2) from the y-axis (in units)?
q.e: The distance from the y-axis is the size of the x-coordinate: |−6| = 6.

q.t: What is the reflection of (3, 5) in the x-axis?
q.e: A mirror along the x-axis flips up and down: the y-coordinate changes sign, x stays.

q.t: What is the reflection of (3, 5) in the y-axis?
q.e: A mirror along the y-axis flips left and right: the x-coordinate changes sign, y stays.

q.t: Find the distance between (2, 3) and (2, −4) (in units).
q.e: Same x, so the segment is vertical: subtract the y's, 3 − (−4) = 7.

q.t: Find the distance between (−3, 1) and (5, 1) (in units).
q.e: Same y, so the segment is horizontal: subtract the x's, 5 − (−3) = 8.

q.t: A point on the x-axis is 5 units to the left of the origin. Its coordinates are:
q.e: On the x-axis means y = 0; left of the origin means x is negative.

q.t: The points (2, 2), (5, 2) and (−1, 2) all lie on a line that is:
q.e: They all have y = 2 — the same height — so they lie on a horizontal line 2 units above the x-axis.

q.t: If the two coordinates of a point have opposite signs, it lies in quadrant:
q.e: (−, +) is Quadrant II and (+, −) is Quadrant IV.

q.t: Find the distance between A (3, 4) and D (7, 1) (in units).
q.e: Sideways shift 4, up-down shift 3; by Baudhāyana–Pythagoras, √(16 + 9) = √25 = 5.

q.t: When is the point (x, y) the same as the point (y, x)?
q.e: Two points are equal only if both coordinates match; swapping makes the first coordinates x and y, equal only when x = y.

q.t: Three feet of a rectangular table are at (8, 9), (11, 9) and (11, 7). Where is the fourth foot?
q.e: A rectangle's missing corner takes the x of one neighbour (8) and the y of the other (7).

q.t: Find the distance from the origin to (6, 8) (in units).
Find the midpoint of the segment joining (−2, 4) and (6, −8).
q.e: Average the x's: (−2 + 6)/2 = 2. Average the y's: (4 − 8)/2 = −2.

q.t: The point (a, b) lies in Quadrant IV. In which quadrant does (−a, −b) lie?
q.e: In IV, a > 0 and b < 0, so −a < 0 and −b > 0: left and up is Quadrant II.

q.t: M (−7, 1) is the midpoint of A (3, −4) and B. Find the x-coordinate of B.
q.e: Other end = 2 × midpoint − known end: 2(−7) − 3 = −17.

q.t: M (−7, 1) is the midpoint of A (3, −4) and B. Find the y-coordinate of B.
Find the distance between D (7, 1) and M (9, 6), to 2 decimal places.
Triangle ADM is reflected in the y-axis. What happens to the lengths of its sides?
q.e: Each x-difference only changes sign, and the distance formula squares it, so every length is unchanged.

q.t: W has x-coordinate −5. Point H is on the line through W parallel to the y-axis. Which must be true?
q.e: A line parallel to the y-axis is vertical: every point on it has the same x-coordinate as W.

q.t: How far is (−5, 12) from the origin (in units)?
q.e: √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13. The negative sign doesn't matter once squared.

q.t: Are M (−3, −4), A (0, 0) and G (6, 8) collinear?
o: No — the distances don't add up
q.e: MA = 5, AG = 10, MG = 15. The two shorter distances add up to the longest, so there is no detour — the points are on one line.

q.t: A (4, 7) and B (16, −2). P is the point of trisection nearer A. Find P.
q.e: Total shift (12, −9); one third of it is (4, −3); A + (4, −3) = (8, 4).

q.t: A (1, −8), B (−4, 7), C (−7, −4) lie on a circle centred at the origin. What is r²?
q.e: Each point is √65 from O: 1 + 64 = 16 + 49 = 49 + 16 = 65.

q.t: For the circle x² + y² = 65 (centre O, radius √65), where is D (−5, 6)?
q.e: 25 + 36 = 61 < 65, so D is closer to O than the radius — inside.

q.t: The midpoints of BC, CA, AB of triangle ABC are D (5, 1), E (6, 5) and F (0, 3). Find A.
A (2, 1), B (−1, 2), C (−2, −1), D (1, −2) form a square. Find its area (in square units).
q.e: Each side is √(9 + 1) = √10 and the diagonals are equal, so it's a square of area (√10)² = 10.

q.t: Circles of radius 80 and 100 have centres (100, 150) and (250, 230). Find the distance between the centres.
For the same two circles (radii 80 and 100, centres 170 apart), what is true?
q.e: If they just touched, the centres would be 180 apart. They are closer than that, so the edges cross.

q.t: Are R (−5, −1), B (−2, −5) and C (4, −12) collinear?
o: No — the step (6, −7) is not a multiple of (3, −4)
No — C is in Quadrant III
q.e: A straight path keeps the same direction, so the steps must be multiples. 6 ÷ 3 = 2 but −7 ÷ −4 = 1.75: the path turns.

q.t: (x, y) is reflected in the x-axis and then in the y-axis. The result is the same as:
q.e: x-axis: (x, −y); then y-axis: (−x, −y). Both signs flip — a half-turn about the origin.
